header.title: Expositio Brevis Antiquae Liturgiae Gallicanae: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Germanus Parisiensis Episcopus
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tmp1223.tmp1223.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.
header.availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1223.tmp1223.opp-lat: Sections are numbered as the edition has them; there is no 1.8. Several words look like scanning errors and were read for sense, e.g. 'lacla' as facta, 'Papis' as panis, 'unum' as uno, 'monitus' as munitus. 1.5: 'suo senio' ('in its old age') is doubtful and may conceal 'suo sinu' ('in its bosom'). 'primum canticum incipiente praesule Ecclesiae' is taken with what follows, reading Ecclesia as subject. The sentence on the three boys is defective: a verb and probably words such as 'the three languages' are missing, so it is marked [...] and breaks off. 1.9: 'in Quinquagesimo' is ambiguous, and the season meant is uncertain. 1.10: 'non' seems to have dropped out before or near 'intercedat', so [no] is supplied. 1.12: 'v. legis lumina' is kept as 'five', though the sense may be disputed; 'dona vi ire' is corrupt and read as dona vitae, 'gifts of life'. 1.13: 'septuaginta quatuor' stands in the text, but the Apocalypse has twenty-four elders, so this is probably an error. 1.15: 'suissed precibus' is read as 'sed suis precibus'. 1.18: 'inrepræhensibilibus' ('irreproachable') is an odd epithet for trumpets, and the text may be unsound.

Line 19: 'Patent' read as 'Patena'; the explanatory 'quia' clause seems to have lost a link to the name (perhaps a play on 'patere'). 'Linostima' is a linen-wool fabric; 'iudumenti' read as 'indumenti'; 'tonica' as 'tunica'. Line 20: the text breaks after 'angelicum canticum' at a footnote mark; 'to sing' is supplied, as is 'is covered' with 'Domini palleo'. Line 21: 'libet' read as 'liber'. Line 22: 'vult augere, ibidem debet addere' is obscure and is rendered with a supplied 'whatever'; 'patiente' lacks a subject, taken as the Lord. Line 23: the sentence 'Nam lieet ... transibunt' is corrupt and appears truncated (the saying presumably continued 'but my words will not pass away'); the rendering is tentative. 'Hoc ergo' read as 'Ideo ergo'. Line 24: 'Qui vivit' is the opening of a closing doxology, left incomplete in the text. The sentence 'Ita pater ... complectet' is uncertain. Antiphons (.2): the edition's corrections 'tanto' and 'compositione' are followed. The text says four kinds but the list is not clearly four. 'Organo' and 'tympano' may be figurative. Line 4: 'vel baptismum quadragesimae non est' is awkward; the sense given is the likely one. Line 5: the Greek word for oil or mercy has dropped out after 'Graece' (presumably a play on elaion/eleos). 'Lucerna' read as plural. Line 6: 'supra scripto die' refers to a day not named in this stretch. The sentence 'ut sicut quando dixit Deus ... appareat' is defective. 'Calicumino/caticumino' read as 'catechumeno'; 'vilati' as 'villato' (napped). The edition marks a gap after 'post modum'. Line 7: the passage on the lentisk is badly broken; words after 'impius' and in the 'risina' sentence are lost, and 'perficitur', 'dispensante' and 'imprimatis' cannot be construed; the gaps are marked. The transition to the Easter material suggests text has fallen out here. Calling balsam a resin of the lentisk is the text's claim. 'Auroris tentae' is unclear, rendered 'first light of dawn'.

Line .8: the opening sentence has no main verb and 'Eucharistia velatus' is ungrammatical; read as 'in which the Eucharist is veiled', which is uncertain. 'Palleum' here seems to be a cloth or veil, not the neck-vestment of line .10.
Line .9: 'prinsecus' is unclear; read as 'intrinsecus' (on the inside), though 'primitus' (from the first) is possible. 'dissimilatum' read as 'distinctive', i.e. unlike ordinary dress.
Line .10: the Isaiah quotation is rendered as this text gives it; 'Palleum laudes' read as 'pallium laudis'.
Lines .11-.12: 'manualia/manicas' is rendered 'cuffs' (detachable sleeve-bands); the exact vestment is disputed. 'vel ut' in .11 is read as 'so that'. In .12 'manica tonica' is read as 'manica tunicam' and the end of the sentence is difficult.
Line .13: 'in alate' read as 'winged'; 'post occasum et volatum' is awkward and possibly corrupt, as is the syntax of 'ex ligno crucis quiescens'.
Line .14: 'veteri' read as 'veteres' (the ancients). 'Sancti a' read as 'Sanctus', though 'Sancta' is possible. The sentence 'angelus in camino flammae in caelis audita est' is broken, since the feminine verb has no subject; words seem to have been lost, and [...] marks this editorially. 'reserantur' is plural and is rendered with 'baptisma' as 'is unlocked'.

nodes.text: BRIEF EXPOSITION OF THE ANCIENT GALLICAN LITURGY BY SAINT GERMANUS, BISHOP OF PARIS. Copied by Dom Martène from a manuscript codex of Saint Martin of Autun, Thesaurus anecdotorum, vol. V.
BRIEF EXPOSITION OF THE ANCIENT GALLICAN LITURGY, ARRANGED IN TWO LETTERS.
FIRST LETTER: HOW THE SOLEMN ORDER OF THE CHURCH IS CARRIED OUT, AND WITH WHAT ARRANGEMENTS THE CHURCH'S CANON IS ADORNED.

Germanus, bishop of Paris, wrote concerning the mass: First, then, and highest of all gifts of grace, the mass is sung in commemoration of the Lord's death, because the death of Christ has become the life of the world, so that by being offered it may avail for the salvation of the living and the rest of the dead.
ON THE *PRELEGERE* [THE OPENING CHANT].

The antiphon for the *prelegendum* is sung in the likeness of those patriarchs who before the Flood thundered forth the coming of Christ in mystical words, as Enoch, the seventh from Adam, who was taken up by God, prophesied, saying: Behold, the Lord comes among his wonderful holy ones to do judgement (Jude 14), and the rest. This testimony the apostle Jude, brother of James, recalls in his Epistle. For just as, while they prophesied, the hand of the Lord came upon the ark, so that among the condemned he might grant a remnant to the earth, so, while the clergy sing psalms, the priest comes forth in the likeness of Christ from the sacristy as if from heaven into the ark of the Lord, which is the Church, so that both by admonishing and by exhorting he may nourish good works in the people and extinguish evil ones.
ON THE SILENCE.

The deacon announces silence for two reasons: namely, that the people, being quiet, may better hear the word of God, and that our heart may be silent from every foul thought, so that the word of God may be better received.

The priest is given to the people for this reason: that when he blesses the people, saying, The Lord be always with you, he may be blessed by all as they say, And with your spirit; so that he may be the more worthy to bless the people, the more, by God's favour, he receives a blessing from the mouth of the whole people.
ON THE *AIUS* [THE GREEK HAGIOS, 'HOLY'].

The *Aius* is sung in the Greek language before the Prophecy for this reason: because the preaching of the New Testament went forth in the world through the Greek language, except for the apostle Matthew, who first published the Gospel of Christ in Judaea in Hebrew letters. Keep, therefore, the honour of the language which first either received the Gospel of Christ in its old age or taught [it] in its own letters. As the first chant, when the bishop begins it, the Church sings the *Aius*, saying [it] in Latin with Greek, to show that the Old and New Testaments are joined. The Amen is said from the Hebrew, after the pattern of the title which, at God's prompting, Pilate set over the cross in three languages, confessing, though unaware, Jesus the Nazarene, that is, Holy and King. The three little boys who with one voice following Kyrie eleison [...] Hebrew, that is, Greek and Latin, or of the three ages of the world, that is, before the law, under the law and under grace,
ON THE PROPHECY.

The canticle of Zechariah the high priest is sung in honour of Saint John the Baptist, because the beginning of salvation consists in the sacrament of baptism, which, by God's gift, began with the ministry of John. And as the shadow of the old [law] was failing and the new brightness of the Gospel was rising, John, standing between them, the last of the prophets and first of the evangelists, shone as a radiant lamp before the face of the true Light. Therefore the Church sings in alternating voices the prophecy which his father sang at his birth.
ON THE PROPHET AND THE APOSTLE.

The prophetic reading, that is, of the Old Testament, keeps its proper order, reproving evils and announcing things to come, so that we may understand that it is the same God who thundered in prophecy, who also taught in the Apostle and shone forth in the splendour of the Gospel.
ON THE APOSTLE.

For what the prophet proclaims as future, the apostle teaches as done. The Acts of the Apostles or the Apocalypse of John are read for the newness of the Easter joy, keeping the order of the seasons, just as the history of the Old Testament [is read] in Quinquagesima, or the deeds of the holy confessors and martyrs on their feast days, so that the people may understand how greatly Christ loved the servant to whom he gave proof of power, and whom the devout common folk ask to be their patron.
ON THE HYMN.

The hymn of the three young men, which is sung after the reading, [is sung] as a figure of the holy ones of old, who sat in darkness awaiting the Lord's coming. For just as, while they were silent, a fourth, an angel, came to them in a cloud of dew and, coming in, overcame the blaze of the fire, so too, while these awaited Christ, the Son of God himself, the Angel of great counsel, came to them, and breaking the dominions of Tartarus, brought them, as he set them free, the joy of the resurrection, as the Evangelist teaches. In accordance with this the Church also keeps the order that between the Benedicite and the Gospel [no] reading should come in, but only a responsory, which is sung by little boys, after the pattern of the Innocents, who, crushed, are read of in the Gospel as sharers in Christ's nativity, or of those children who, as the Lord was hastening to his passion, cried out in the temple, Hosanna, Son of David, as the Psalmist sings: Out of the mouth of infants and sucklings you have perfected praise (Ps. 8:3).
ON THE *AIUS* BEFORE THE GOSPEL.

Then, at the coming of the holy Gospel, the clergy sing the *Aius* again in clear melody, in the likeness of the angels crying out before the face of Christ at the gates of hell: Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the Lord of hosts, the king of glory, shall enter (Ps. 23:7).
ON THE GOSPEL.

The procession of the holy Gospel goes forth like the power of Christ triumphing over death, with the aforesaid harmonies and with seven candlesticks of light, which are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, or the five lights of the law fixed to the mystery of the cross. It ascends the tribunal of the *analogium* [the lectern], as Christ [ascended] the seat of the Father's kingdom, so that from there it may thunder forth the gifts of life, while the clergy cry out, Glory to you, O Lord, in the likeness of the angels who, at the Lord's birth, sang Glory to God in the highest (Luke 2:14), appearing to the shepherds.
ON THE SANCTUS AFTER THE GOSPEL.

The Sanctus, which the clergy sing as the holy Gospel returns, [is sung] in the likeness of the saints who, when the Lord Jesus Christ returned from the underworld, sang a canticle of praise as they followed the Lord, or of the seventy-four elders whom John recalls in the Apocalypse, who, casting their crowns before the Lamb, sang a sweet canticle.
ON HOMILIES.

The homilies of the saints that are read are appointed solely for preaching, so that whatever the prophet, the Apostle or the Gospel has commanded, the teacher or pastor of the Church may preach to the people in plainer speech, tempering it with such skill that neither does rusticity offend the wise nor does refined eloquence become obscure to the rustic.
ON THE PRAYER.

That the Levites sing prayers for the people takes its origin from the beginning, from the books of Moses, so that when the preaching of the apostles has been heard, the Levites may pray for the people and the priests, prostrate before the Lord, may intercede for the sins of the people, as the Lord says to Aaron: You and your sons and all the tribe of Levi shall bear the sins of my people, that is, not by enduring them as a penalty, but by lifting them up with their prayers.
ON THE CATECHUMEN.

The deacon therefore calls out for the catechumen according to the ancient rite of the Church, so that Jews as well as heretics or pagans under instruction, who used to come to baptism as adults and were tested before baptism, might stand in the church and hear the counsel of the Old and New Testaments; that afterward the Levites might pray for them and the priest say the collect; and that after the prayer they, not being worthy to stand [there] while the offering was brought in, might then go out and listen outside before the door, prostrate on the ground, to the great works [of God]. This duty belonged to the deacon or to the doorkeeper: that the one should admonish them to go out and the other see to it that no unworthy person lingered in the temple, saying: Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine. For what on earth is holier than the making of the body and blood of Christ, and what is more unclean than a dog and a pig? To these by likeness is to be compared the one who either has not been cleansed by baptism or has not been fortified by the seal of the cross.

Spiritually we are commanded to keep silence, watching at the door, that is, that being quiet from the tumult of words or of vices we may set the sign of the cross before our face, so that desire may not enter through the eyes, nor anger through the ear, so that foul speech may not come forth from the lips, and so that the heart may strive for this alone, to receive Christ into itself.
ON THE *SONUS* [THE OFFERTORY CHANT].

The *Sonus*, which is sung when the offering comes forward, took its beginning from this. The Lord commanded Moses to make silver trumpets, which the Levites were to sound when the victim was offered, and this was to be the sign by which the people might understand at what hour the offering was being brought in, and all, bowed down, were to adore the Lord until the pillar of fire or the cloud should come to bless the sacrifice. But now, as the body of Christ comes forward to the altar, no longer with irreproachable trumpets but with spiritual voices, the Church sings the glorious great works of Christ in sweet melody. The body of the Lord is carried in towers for this reason: because the Lord's tomb was cut in the rock in the likeness of a tower, and inside was the bed where the Lord's body rested, from which the King of glory rose in triumph. The blood of Christ is specially offered in a chalice for this reason: because in such a vessel the mystery of the Eucharist was consecrated on the day before the Lord suffered, as he himself said: This is the chalice of my blood, the mystery of faith, which shall be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins (Matt. 26:28). The bread is transformed into body and the wine into blood, as the Lord says of his body: For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink (John 6:55). Of the bread he said, This is my body, and of the wine, This is my blood (Matt. 26:26). Water is mixed in for this reason: either because it is fitting for the people to be united with the Lord, or because blood and water flowed from Christ's side on the cross, so that by the one we may be cleansed from the stain of sins, and by the other be prepared for the kingdom of heaven.

It is called a paten, where the offering is consecrated, because the mystery of the Eucharist is offered in commemoration of the Lord's passion. The *palla linostima* [a cloth of linen and wool] holds the figure of that garment which, woven all around, was not divided by the soldiers, namely the tunic of Christ. The corporal pall, on which the offering is placed, is of pure linen for this reason: because the Lord's body was wrapped in pure linen cloths with spices in the tomb. The covering of the sacraments is adorned for this reason: because the resurrection of Christ surpasses all adornments, or [it signifies] the vault of heaven, which now hides the Lord from our eyes. The silk is adorned with gold or gems because the Lord commanded Moses that veils be made in the tabernacle of gold, blue, and purple, and twice-dyed scarlet and twisted fine linen: because all those mysteries went before the marks of Christ.

The Lauds, that is, the Alleluia, John in the Apocalypse heard being sung after the resurrection. Therefore at that hour, when the Lord [is covered] with the pall, as Christ is covered by heaven, the Church is accustomed [to sing] the angelic canticle: and the fact that the Alleluia itself has a first, a second and a third [part] signifies the three times: before the law, under the law, under grace.

The names of the dead are recited at that hour when the pall is taken off, because the resurrection of the dead will take place then, when at Christ's coming heaven will be folded up like a book. They exchange the peace of Christ with one another so that by a mutual kiss they may keep within themselves the affection of love, and so that whoever is darkened by any discord may quickly hasten back to grace, or ask pardon of his neighbour, lest by giving a false peace he incur fellowship with the traitor, and so that the Eucharist received or the blessing given may profit the more, the more Christ sees hearts to be peaceable; for he himself commanded the disciples as he ascended to heaven: Peace I leave with you, my peace I give to you (John 14:27), and: By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another.

The priest admonishes [us] to lift up our hearts so that no earthly thought may remain in our breasts at the hour of the sacred offering, and so that Christ may be received the better in the mind, the more the thought strives to attend to him alone. The fraction and commingling of the Lord's body was shown in ancient times to the holy Fathers with such great mysteries that, while the priest was breaking the offering, it seemed as if an angel of God were cutting up the limbs of a shining boy with a knife and catching his blood in the chalice to collect it, so that they might speak more truly the word in which the Lord says that his flesh is food and his blood is drink. At this fraction, whatever the priest wishes to add he must add at this very point, because at that moment heavenly things are mingled with earthly, and at the priest's prayer the heavens are opened. While the priest is breaking [the offering], the clergy fill [the time] by singing an antiphon, because while [the Lord] suffered the pain of death all the elements trembled and bore witness.

The Lord's Prayer is placed at this very point so that all our prayer may be closed in the Lord's Prayer. That priests should pour out a blessing on the people the Lord commanded through Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and to his sons; thus you shall bless the people: May [the Lord] bless you and keep you (Num. 6:23), and the rest that follows. So Aaron bore the place of Christ, and his sons the place of the presbyters. The Lord therefore commanded both to bless the people; but to preserve the honour of the bishop, the sacred canons have laid down that a bishop should pronounce a longer blessing and a presbyter pour out a shorter one, saying: Peace, faith and love and the communion of the body and blood of the Lord be always with you. For that blessing which God dictated to Moses is permitted, and no one can gainsay a presbyter [in it]; because heaven and earth will pass away. Therefore the blessing is given before communion, so that the mystery of blessing may enter a blessed vessel. How sweet the holy communion of soul and body is, Christ shows in the words of the Gospel, saying: If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, whatever you ask of the Father in my name will be done for you (John 15:7).

The *Trecanum* [the threefold chant] that is sung is a sign that the catholic faith proceeds from belief in the Trinity. For thus the first [part] turns into the second, the second into the third, and again the third into the second and the second into the first. So the Father in the Son encompasses the mystery of the Trinity: the Father in the Son, the Son in the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit in the Son, and the Son again in the Father. But now let this letter come to an end, in which the solemn Order is shown, set out briefly, so that in the letter to follow, by the Lord's gift, [what concerns] the common office may be opened to your ears. Who lives.
HERE BEGINS THE SECOND LETTER, ON THE COMMON OFFICE. I

Since, by the Lord's favour, we have briefly gone over in the earlier letter the order of the sacred offering, to explain it, let us now set down in a short little page on what principle the various gifts of the Church stand, according to what the Lord grants us to understand.

The antiphons which the Church sings with sweet ceremony took their beginning from this. When King Solomon had built the most renowned house, he appointed singers there, who were to sing the great works of God with various instruments, so that among the other adornments that shone in the temple, the divine words too might be delivered in sweet speech, so that the word of God might give delight so much the more, the more elegantly it was rolled forth with the adornment of the voice. For the custom of singing was established in the church for the sake of the carnal, not for the sake of the spiritual, so that those who are not pricked to the heart by words may be moved by the sweetness of melody, considering how great the sweetness of the heavenly song is, when in the sojourn of this world the Church sounds forth the praises of Christ so elegantly. It is called an antiphon because it is placed before first, and then the verse of the psalm is placed, while the glory of the Trinity is joined on. There are four kinds of them, composed with the organ from the prophetic [writings], with the drum from the sacred thunder of the Gospel, or by the composition of the catholic Fathers according to the order of the seasons, either by entreating, or by narrating, or by drumming out divine praises.

The responsories that are sung in the divine offices by day or night took their origin from the Pentateuch of Moses, when, after Pharaoh was drowned, Miriam the prophetess, taking a drum, led the canticle, and the people gathered in a choir responded. Their rationale is fourfold, as is contained above about the antiphons. The custom of leading and responding is shown not only at the Red Sea, but among many tribes of the Hebrews, as the history of the Old Testament relates more fully.

*Sanctus Deus archangelorum* [Holy God of the archangels] is sung in Lent, and not the canticle of Zechariah, because this melody is one of supplication for the people, as the words of the text itself contain. And for this reason the Prophecy is not sung, and for the same reason the baptistery too is closed; namely because the canons prescribe that there is no baptism in Lent.

The oil that is blessed together with the chrism is shown by the voice of the psalm which is uttered concerning Christ (Ps. 44:8): God has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions, or this: With my holy oil I have anointed him (Ps. 88:21); so first they were anointed with the old oil, and then they were drenched with ointment. In particular, oil in Greek is called in Latin mercy, and by oil the grace of the Holy Spirit is designated. For God consecrated this liquid in the Church for preparing mystical ointments, or for making ready lamps, or for soothing the wounds of sins.

The Creed is handed over to the *competentes* [candidates for baptism] on the day written above for this reason: so that, as when God said Let there be light, what signifies the illumination of belief may appear. On the seventh day he blessed and sanctified [it] in rest: therefore on this day the faith of the people is strengthened, by the Creed and the milk of chrism it is nourished, because on the seventh day the rest of Christ in the tomb is observed, and as the day draws to its close the triumph of his resurrection is consecrated. And when the priest comes to hand over the Creed, soft feather [cushions] and white towels are spread out over the chancel rail, and small vessels of chrism and of oil, to be blessed, are brought in chalices, and the book of the holy Gospel covered with a red veil, because the people coming to faith holds the figure of infancy. For as an infant is tender and new in body, so a catechumen is tender and new in the faith. The infant's limbs are laid on feather cushions so that he may be better nurtured. To the catechumen the gentle words of the Lord are delivered, so that he may be delighted the more. For he cannot bear stronger precepts before he is confirmed in grace through the baptism of the Holy Spirit. The little one's limbs are wiped with towels, that is, with white and napped linen, so that his skin may not be harmed. So to the catechumen the subtlety of the faith is opened in the Creed, so that through belief he may be wiped clean of all sin. First gently, through gentle precepts, so that he may not be chafed, being tender in understanding; afterwards [...] through stronger commandments, so that he may grow strong through works. The infant is nourished with milk, and the catechumen is anointed with chrism. Milk is sucked from the mother's breasts, and chrism is consecrated in the bosom of holy Mother Church.

The book of the Gospel, in the likeness of the body of Christ, is covered with a red veil, the sign of blood showing it. The vessels of chrism are brought in chalices because all the sacraments of baptism are made firm in the passion of Christ. The glass or crystal vessels of chrism signify the brightness of baptism. Chrism is made with balsam. The *lentiscus* [lentisk or mastic] is said to be a kind of tree from which balsam resin is taken; of this lentisk, it is handed down, was that part of the Lord's cross where the impious one fixed the holy hands of the Lord with a nail, [...] is accomplished. And therefore the resin of that tree, by the dispensation [...] even from ancient times, first of all [...] is poured in. For the angel of God descends at the secret [prayers] upon the altar as upon the tomb, and blesses the host itself, in the manner of that angel who announced the good news of Christ's resurrection. Then with free tongue and clear voice all the canticles that were shut away in silence during Lent are taken up again, both the drowning of Pharaoh and the *Sanctus de caelis* [Holy from the heavens] and the Alleluia with joys, because the Lord has risen. It is completed in the office at midnight, because at midnight the Saviour broke hell; then the flesh of the Lamb is eaten by the mouth of the faithful people, and the blood is sweetly drunk, by which the whole world is redeemed at a glorious price, and at once it is taught that at the first light of dawn the praise of the Lord's resurrection is to be celebrated with clear song and with blessings.

The pall with little bells, in which the Eucharist is veiled at Easter, [is] after the pattern of the Old Testament, where the priest's tunic is shown full of little bells, signifying the words of preaching. The girding of the white garment with which the priest about to baptize is girded is done as a sign of Saint John, who, being girded, baptized the Lord. White garments are put on at Easter, according as the angel was seen at the tomb in white garments. For white garments signify exultation.

The chasuble, which they call the *amphibalus* [a closed outer vestment], which the priest puts on, all of one piece, is shown to have been first instituted through Moses the lawgiver. For the Lord commanded a distinctive garment to be made, so that the priest should put on such a one as the people would not dare to put on. It is without sleeves for this reason, because the priest blesses rather than serves. It is of one piece on the inside for this reason, not cut, not open, because there are many secret mysteries of sacred Scripture which the learned priest ought to hide as if under a seal, and to guard the unity of the faith, and not to turn aside into heresy or schisms.

The pallium, which goes around the neck and comes down to the breast, was called the *rationale* [the priest's breastplate] in the Old Testament, that is, a sign of holiness over the memory of the breast, as the prophet says in the person of the Lord: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me. And a little later: That I might set glory for those who mourn Zion, and give them a crown in place of ashes, the oil of joy in place of mourning (Isa. 61:3). A pallium of praise in place of a spirit of sorrow. That it encircles the neck is of ancient custom, because kings and priests were wrapped in a pallium, a shining garment, which foreshadowed grace. That fringes are attached to priestly vestments, the Lord commanded Moses in Numbers, that the children of Israel should make fringes at the four corners of their pallia, so that the people of the Lord should bear the sign of God's commandments not only in deed but also in clothing.

*Manualia*, that is, cuffs, it is the custom for priests to put on, after the pattern of the armlets by which the arms of kings or priests were bound. They are made of any precious cloth, and not of hard metal, for this reason: so that all priests in common, even those of lesser standing in the world, may find them more easily.

It is a small garment, which is to be for no other use except for frequenting the sacrifice, and it signifies that our hands are not to be weighed down by the honours of the world, but are to be girded with the subtle exercises of God's commandments. The cuff keeps the tunic from showing as a cheap garment, or from any unworthy touch of filth [coming] upon the divine sacrifices, where the hands that offer [them] move about.

The albs that the Levites use the fathers established for this reason, because on a dyed garment a stain does not show as quickly as on a white one; and the minister of the altar uses it so that he may watch for and avoid every stain, and so that the garments of those who minister may in no way appear soiled by even the lightest touch, but may be white, outwardly in clothing, inwardly in mind. It is made of silk or of wool, because the Lord commanded priests to have vestments from these materials for this reason, that their clothing might show the hope of the resurrection. For silk is made on a tree by a worm. The worm after death comes forth winged, and after its setting and flight it figures Christ, who, resting from the wood of the cross in the tomb like a worm shut in a narrow little bag, rose from the grave and took flight to the heavens. An alb of the other cloth shows only innocence of life. The alb is not bound with a belt, but hangs free and covers the Levite's body, because the whole Levitical way of life, in desire for the heavenly homeland, ought to be held free from earthly works, and not bound by the belt of sins.

The stole that the deacon puts on over the alb signifies a subtle understanding of the divine mysteries, although the ancients, putting on the stole, showed that they had the joy of a solemn feast. And for this reason it is not used in Lent, for humiliation, just as in our Church neither the Alleluia, the Sanctus, the Prophecy, the hymn of the three youths, nor the canticle of the Red Sea are sung on those days. For an angel appeared girded with a white stole when, sitting at the Lord's tomb, he announced the solemn feast of his resurrection. Therefore these canticles are to be forbidden in Lent, because they are heavenly and angelic. For from the heavens [came] the pillar of fire by night and the pillar of cloud by day, the angel in the furnace of flame [...] was heard in the heavens. So the Alleluia and the Sanctus are kept silent in penitence, so that they may become new at the Lord's Resurrection, when baptism too is unlocked. Therefore the Levite must sing the heavenly canticle.
